extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and judges (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards for applying the doctrine of equivalents, defining claim scope, and determining when disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter is dedicated to the public; guidance on related prosecution remedies (reissue/continuation) and limits on expanding claim scope. Intended to guide courts and practitioners in infringement and claim-drafting/prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent claims give notice of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims give notice of the scope of patent protection, giving notice both to the examiner at the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) during prosecution, and to the public at large, including potential competitors, after the patent has issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims perform a notice function to PTO examiners and the public; this underpins many limitations on post-issuance expansion of scope (citations: Aro Mfg., Continental Paper Bag Co., Mahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims, not specification, measure patentee's right
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent claims, not the specification, provide the measure of the patentee’s right to exclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the specification teaches and may limit claim interpretation, it cannot be used to expand the scope of the claims; 'Specifications teach. Claims claim.' (citations and historical authorities included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare accused product to claims as construed (not to preferred embodiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of patent infringement compares the accused product with the claims as construed by the court; infringement, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents, does not arise by comparing the accused product with a preferred embodiment described in the specification, or with a commercialized embodiment of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base infringement findings on similarities to embodiments in the specification; focus on claim construction and element-by-element comparison (SRI Int’l cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's subjective intent irrelevant to dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee’s subjective intent is irrelevant to determining whether unclaimed subject matter has been disclosed and therefore dedicated to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedication is an objective legal determination based on the disclosure and claims, not on what the patentee intended or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure without claiming dedicates subject matter to the public (Maxwell rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent drafter discloses but declines to claim subject matter, this action dedicates that unclaimed subject matter to the public, and application of the doctrine of equivalents to recapture subject matter deliberately left unclaimed would conflict with the primacy of the claims in defining the scope of the patentee’s exclusive right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes an alternative and the patentee elects not to claim it, courts will treat that unclaimed alternative as dedicated to the public and unavailable to be recovered via the doctrine of equivalents; this avoids encouraging applicants to disclose broadly but file narrow claims to evade examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may not narrow claims to avoid PTO scrutiny then recapture via DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot narrowly claim an invention to avoid prosecution scrutiny by the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO), and then, after patent issuance, use the doctrine of equivalents to establish infringement because the specification discloses equivalents; such a result would encourage presenting a broad disclosure and filing narrow claims to avoid examination of broader claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts enforce Maxwell-type rules to prevent strategic narrowing during prosecution followed by post-issuance broadening through equivalents; prosecution history and disclosure are relevant to this determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se bar for disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter (holding applied to facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that specifically limits claims to 'a sheet of aluminum' but whose specification discloses that 'other metals, such as stainless steel ... may be used' cannot invoke the doctrine of equivalents to extend its aluminum limitation to encompass steel; disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter is dedicated to the public (this decision overrules YBM Magnex to that extent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On these facts the court held as a matter of law that equivalency was unavailable where the specification disclosed the unclaimed substitute; practitioners should not expect DOE to reach combinations explicitly disclosed but omitted from the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for inadvertently unclaimed disclosed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who inadvertently fails to claim disclosed subject matter may, within two years from the grant of the original patent, file a reissue application and attempt to enlarge the scope of the original claims (35 U.S.C. § 251), or file a separate (continuation) application claiming the disclosed subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 120 if filed before all applications in the chain issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory avenues (reissue and continuation/priority remedies) are the proper means to obtain coverage for disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter rather than relying on the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents: context-sensitive limitation (Graver Tank/Warner–Jenkinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents extends the right to exclude beyond the literal scope of the claims, but 'equivalency must be determined against the context of the patent, the prior art, and the particular circumstances of the case.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE remains available in appropriate cases, but its application must avoid significant conflict with the fundamental principle that claims define patent limits; consider prior art, degree of invention, and case-specific facts when applying DOE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel and amendments (Warner–Jenkinson guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment during prosecution (e.g., adding a lower limit) may make an element material to the claim, but that fact alone does not necessarily preclude the application of the doctrine of equivalents to that element; courts must inquire into the patentee’s reason for the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim language was narrowed during prosecution, evaluate why the amendment was made (e.g., to avoid prior art or for other reasons) before concluding that estoppel bars equivalents for that element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element requirement for DOE (Pennwalt principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect the notice function of claims, courts require an equivalent for each and every element of a claim rather than applying the doctrine of equivalents to the claim as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply DOE on a limitation-by-limitation basis; the absence of an equivalent for any required element weighs against a finding of non-literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed foreseeability test (alternative reasoning in concurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative reconciling principle proposed by concurrence: the doctrine of equivalents does not capture subject matter that the patent drafter reasonably could have foreseen during the application process and included in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foreseeability-based approach would enhance the notice function by treating as outside DOE any subject matter that was reasonably foreseeable to the drafter and therefore could have been claimed; it is offered as an alternative standard for courts to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festo / surrender during prosecution bars expansion for surrendered subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To enhance notice, courts propose to bar patentees from expanding their claim to embrace subject matter surrendered during the patent acquisition process (prosecution history estoppel/surrender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claim amendments or arguments during prosecution amounted to surrender of claim scope; surrendered matter cannot later be reclaimed under DOE.
